analysis.one_liner: Requires small business lenders to disclose the true annual cost of loans, advances, and factoring deals to borrowers.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced in June 2023 and referred to the House Financial Services Committee, where no further action was ever taken before Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: Small businesses that borrow money do not get the same price disclosures that consumers get on a credit card or mortgage. This bill would change that: any lender offering a small business a loan, line of credit, merchant cash advance, or factoring deal of $2.5 million or less would have to state, in writing at the time of the offer, the full annual percentage rate including fees, the payment amounts, the term, prepayment costs, and collateral requirements. It would also stop lenders from charging a new fee on the outstanding balance when they refinance a fixed-fee loan, and it would give the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau authority over small business financing products.
analysis.who_benefits: Small business owners — restaurants, retailers, contractors, and other Main Street firms — seeking financing of $2.5 million or less. Today, a merchant cash advance or factoring deal is often quoted as a "factor rate" or a daily payment with no annual percentage rate, so a borrower cannot easily compare a 1.3 factor rate to a 25% APR bank loan or see what they are actually paying. The bill would force every offer to show a true annual percentage rate including fees, itemize the finance charge, disclose prepayment penalties and collateral requirements, and prevent lenders from collecting a second fee when refinancing. This covers the millions of small firms that consumer lending law leaves unprotected.

how_it_helps.text: It applies the Truth in Lending Act — the law that forces consumer lenders to show an annual percentage rate — to small business financing of $2.5 million or less.

Lenders would have to disclose, at the time of a binding offer: the financing amount after fees, the APR including unavoidable fees, payment amounts and frequency, the term, a broken-down finance charge, prepayment costs, and any collateral requirement.

It bars lenders from charging a new fee on the outstanding principal when refinancing a fixed-fee loan unless there is a tangible benefit to the borrower — ending the practice of collecting the same fee twice on a refinanced loan.
It requires that whenever a lender states any rate in writing, it must also state the APR with equal or greater prominence, so less flattering metrics cannot be used to obscure the true cost.
It gives the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau the same oversight authority over small business financing that it has over consumer financial products.

analysis.who_pays: Lenders offering small business financing — especially online and nonbank lenders, merchant cash advance companies, and factoring companies whose pricing is often opaque — would bear the cost of calculating and disclosing annual percentage rates and itemized fees, and would lose revenue from double-dipping on refinanced loans and from borrowers who can now comparison shop and walk away from expensive offers. Some of that cost could be passed on to borrowers in prices.
analysis.who_pays_short: Nonbank small business and MCA lenders

drawbacks.text: Lenders would face new compliance costs to calculate and disclose APRs across varied products (loans, lines of credit, sales-based advances, factoring), which could be passed on to borrowers as higher prices or fewer product options.
For sales-based financing and factoring, the APR must be an estimate based on projected sales or historical payment periods, which may not match what a borrower actually pays if revenue swings.
The bill would not take effect until three years after enactment, with rules due at two years, so any protection would be delayed even if it had passed.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit is real and well-targeted: the same plain-language APR rules that protect consumers would apply to small business loans, closing a gap that lets lenders quote factor rates and daily payments that hide triple-digit annual costs. The honest drawbacks are the compliance cost, which small and nonbank lenders would bear and likely pass through to borrowers; the imprecision of an "estimated APR" for sales-based financing, which depends on projecting a business's future sales; and the long runway — rules due two years after enactment, no effect until three years — meaning relief would have been slow even had it passed. On balance, the transparency benefit for borrowers outweighs the compliance burden.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the House Financial Services Committee the day it was introduced, and the committee never took it up before the two-year Congress ended, so no one ever got to vote on it.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced in the House on June 15, 2023 and referred to the House Committee on Financial Services the same day.
The committee took no further action — no hearing, no markup, no vote — and the bill was never reported to the House floor.
The 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025 with the bill still sitting in committee, so it expired.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Small business lenders who sell loans, merchant cash advances, and factoring deals without disclosing an annual percentage rate are better off — their pricing stays opaque, and business owners cannot easily compare their products to a plain APR. The committee chair who never scheduled a vote also avoided a contested vote on an anti-gouging bill.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Nonbank and online small business lenders

against.name: House Committee on Financial Services (chaired by Rep. Patrick McHenry)
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on the day it was introduced and took no further action — no hearing, no markup, no vote — for the remaining 18 months of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken; the bill's only recorded support came from two House Democrats, and no Republican acted on it either way.

industries.industry: Online and nonbank small business lenders (including merchant cash advance and sales-based financing companies)
industries.note: These lenders profit from products sold with factor rates, daily payment schedules, and other metrics that don't translate into an annual rate. Being forced to disclose an APR including all fees would make their pricing comparable and likely cut the rates they can charge.

Factoring — buying a business's unpaid invoices at a discount — would have to disclose an estimated APR including the discount taken, making what has traditionally been an opaque cost explicit. Businesses selling invoices would see the true annual cost of the money they receive.

industries.industry: Banks and established small business lenders
industries.note: Banks already make loan cost disclosures and would face some adjustment, but the new standardized APR comparison would also apply to their competitors, leveling the field. Borrowers would be able to compare bank loans against nonbank products on the same terms.
